g.text: five bytes, MSB first; each bit is a WIDTH, not a level
The start signal is the longest single timed interval in the project.
18 ms = 1.08 million clocks - 6.4 times the WS2812 reset and 900 times the
WS2812 bit cell - so it is what forces a three-level delay routine rather than
a NOP sled, and it is on the (6,255) pair whose outer step is 5 145 clocks
Why the host PULLS HIGH before releasing, which is not optional.
The DHT11 pulls its own line LOW to answer, so the
host cannot simply stop driving and let the pull-up
win: the sensor would see a line that never went
high and would not start converting. Pulling it high
for 30 us guarantees a clean high-to-low transition
to answer with, and only then does the host become a
It is also the one place this program drives the line
high push-pull into a device that may pull it low,
which is safe only because the host has already
stopped driving by the time the sensor answers.
Why the acknowledgement is skipped rather than timed.
Nothing on the wire announces when the acknowledge is
over, so timing it would be another delay constant to
fit and another place to be wrong. Instead the firmware
falls into the same edge-wait loop it uses for bits:
the first round waits out the 80/80 us acknowledge and
the second one is bit 0. One loop, two uses.
Why the firmware records the checksum instead of checking it.
A program that silently drops a bad frame is a program
whose failure is invisible - it looks like a sensor
that has gone quiet. So the byte is banked in dmem[4]
and the CHECK is left to whoever reads it, here the
testbench. The firmware's job is to be faithful to the
wire; the decision about what to do about it belongs
this one reads once and parks
|= bit |= sensor: low | sensor: release | total | the host samples at 45 us into the release |=
(the SHORT end of the 26-28 us window - a sensor inside its own spec)
the line is already LOW again: 17 us of margin
the line is still HIGH: 25 us of margin
The bit PERIOD is not fixed
- 76..78 us for a 0 and 120 us for a 1 - and that is
the whole reason the host synchronises on edges instead of counting. At the 2 us
spread of the 0-bit, twenty zero bits is 40 us of slip against a 17 us margin: a
counting host tracks the nominal frame perfectly and then fails on a sensor that
THE SAMPLE CANNOT GO INSIDE THE RELEASE.
A line high 20 us into the release
is a 0 AND a 1. The two differ only afterwards, so the sample is aimed at the
45 us point where a 0 has already ended and a 1 has not.
There is no 9th bit, no parity and no framing.
